title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a cowshed at dawn, smoke and jasmine in the same breath, and a goddess whose doorway is fragrance

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Sukta gave misfortune a face, Alakshmi, and the singer helped show her the door.

A village before sunrise smells like several things at once. Woodsmoke. Wet earth. Milk warming in a pot. The cowshed, which nobody would call perfume. And then, from somewhere, a string of jasmine on a doorframe. Every one of those smells means the household is alive: fuel, food, animals fed, someone who cared enough to hang flowers. Today's lines of the Sri Sukta smell like that morning. The riches they name start in the cowshed and end in a person's mouth.
screen: `WOODSMOKE, WET EARTH, WARM MILK.` → `THE COWSHED, AND JASMINE.` → `A HOUSEHOLD THAT'S ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Her doorway is fragrance. She is hard to overcome, always flourishing, rich in cow dung, the queen of all beings: I call Sri near. Yes, rich in cow dung. It's there in the Sanskrit, karishini, right next to queen of all beings, and the hymn sees no contradiction. In a farming household, dung is fuel for the fire, food for the fields and plaster for the floor. It means the cattle are healthy and the soil will feed you. So the goddess of fortune smells of jasmine at the door and of the cowshed out back, and both are signs of her. Now the next line, which goes somewhere else entirely. In paraphrase: may we gain the wish of the mind, the intention of the heart, the truth of speech. The beauty of cattle, and of food. May Sri and good name rest in me. First it asks for things nobody can store in a barn: the mind's wish fulfilled, an intention carried through, truth in what you say. In a hymn about fortune, truth of speech is counted as riches. Some readers hear the two lines as a pair. One is the outer household: animals, fuel, fields, a fragrant door. The other is the inner one: a clear mind, a kept intention, honest words. And the hymn asks that Sri rest in the person, not only in the barn. Others simply hear a full life, described from the ground up. Either way, the fortune this hymn wants is wider than money, and earthier, and it includes the way a person talks.
screen: `HER DOORWAY IS FRAGRANCE.` · `RICH IN COW DUNG, QUEEN OF ALL.` · `THE WISH, THE INTENTION, THE TRUTH.` · `MAY SRI REST IN ME.` · then, large: `TRUTH OF SPEECH, COUNTED AS RICHES.`

segments.voice: Notice the earthy riches around you, the air, a roof, water within reach, one per breath. Then turn inward: an intention you've been carrying, something true you said this week, and let that count too. If you pray, you can give thanks to the goddess, or to God, for both; if you don't, let yourself be a little richer than you thought.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that calls Sri fragrant at the door and rich in cow dung, and asks for truth of speech in the same breath as cattle and food.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Jasmine at the door, the cowshed out back, and an honest word. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: In some Hindu homes, especially in villages, cattle are honored at festivals and floors and courtyards are freshly plastered and decorated before Lakshmi worship; the Sri Sukta is chanted as part of that worship.

chat.says: Does the Sri Sukta only ask for money and cattle?
options: No: beside cattle and food it asks for truth of speech, and counts that as riches too.
Yes, it asks only for gold and cattle, and says nothing about the inner life.
No, it turns down cattle and dung as unclean, and asks only for clean gold.
chat.meaning: The hymn calls Sri rich in cow dung, queen of all beings, and asks for the mind's wish, a kept intention and truth of speech among the riches.

karishini.meaning: rich in cow dung, a sign of a thriving farm

Sri Sukta.meaning: the hymn to Sri, the goddess of fortune

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 9–10 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)

notes: Verse 9 paraphrased: gandhadvārāṃ durādharṣāṃ nityapuṣṭāṃ karīṣiṇīm / īśvarīṃ sarvabhūtānāṃ tām ihopahvaye śriyam. karīṣiṇī glossed 'rich in cow dung' (karīṣa, dried dung); some translators soften it to 'abounding in cattle wealth'. Confirm the plain rendering is acceptable for this audience.
Verse 10 paraphrased: manasaḥ kāmam ākūtiṃ vācaḥ satyam aśīmahi / paśūnāṃ rūpam annasya mayi śrīḥ śrayatāṃ yaśaḥ. ākūti glossed 'intention of the heart'; yaśas as 'good name'. Confirm.
Uses of dung (fuel, fertilizer, floor plaster) are given as everyday rural practice, not tied to the text; confirm.
The two readings (outer and inner household; a full life described from the ground up) are offered without ranking.
